stories.headline: OCTOBER HIKE ODDS HIT 71% AS FED PIVOTS FROM CUTS TO HIKES
stories.body: CME FedWatch odds of a second-straight rate hike at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting rose to 71%, up from 66% a day earlier and just 8.8% a month ago. The Fed already raised its target range 25 bps to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16 in its first hike since 2023, with 16 of 18 policymakers penciling in at least one more before year-end.
stories.explain: A rate hike two meetings in a row, arriving months after the Fed was still cutting, means the committee sees inflation re-accelerating faster than growth is slowing — exactly the scenario that forces central banks to reverse course quickly. Because Fed funds futures reprice continuously between meetings, that 71% probability already flows straight into every other yield on the curve well before October 28, which is why bond and equity markets are responding today rather than waiting three weeks.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HOLDS NEAR 19-YEAR HIGH, 30-YEAR TOPS LEVELS UNSEEN SINCE 2004
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield was little changed at 5.17%, a whisker below Thursday's 19-year high, while the 30-year sits near 5.50%, its highest since 2004, and the 2-year holds around 4.80%. The pause follows a week-long selloff driven by hawkish Fed commentary, elevated energy prices, and a hot PMI report.
stories.explain: Long yields stalling rather than reversing signals the market isn't fighting the repriced hike path — it's digesting it. The 30-year's move is the more telling one: it's driven mostly by term premium (compensation for holding duration risk) rather than near-term Fed expectations, so its rise to a 22-year high reflects investors demanding more compensation for uncertainty about where inflation and deficits land over the next three decades, not just where rates sit next quarter.

stories.headline: DOW JUMPS 478 POINTS, STOCKS NOTCH WEEKLY GAINS DESPITE BOND SELLOFF
stories.body: The Dow rose 478.64 points (+0.93%) to 51,828.62, the S&P 500 gained 0.51% to 7,743.41, and the Nasdaq added 0.5%, with all three snapping the Dow's three-week losing streak on a weekly basis (S&P +0.7%, Nasdaq +1.6%) as oil prices eased and the Treasury selloff paused.
stories.explain: Equities rallying on the same day yields merely stopped rising — rather than needing yields to actually fall — shows how much of this month's stock weakness was a rate-of-change story: markets sell off hardest while repricing is happening, then stabilize once the new hike odds are fully absorbed into prices, even if the absolute yield level stays elevated.

stories.headline: OIL SLIDES 2.2% AS SUPPLY FEARS EASE, TAKING PRESSURE OFF STOCKS
stories.body: WTI crude fell 2.2% to $92.55 a barrel Friday, its first meaningful pullback after a month-long, 40%-plus run driven largely by the Iran-linked Strait of Hormuz standoff, giving equity markets room to rally as one of the two big macro headwinds this week (oil and yields) finally loosened its grip.
stories.explain: Crude carries a geopolitical risk premium on top of physical supply-and-demand fundamentals whenever a chokepoint like Hormuz is contested, and that premium can compress quickly on any de-escalation signal even without a change in actual barrels flowing. Lower oil also feeds directly into headline CPI, so today's pullback modestly eases the same inflation math that's been pushing the Fed toward more hikes.

stories.headline: CONSUMER SENTIMENT SINKS TO 48.1 AS INFLATION EXPECTATIONS JUMP TO 4.6%
stories.body: The University of Michigan's final September sentiment index fell to 48.1 from August's 51.7 (-7% month-over-month) and 12.7% below year-ago levels, while the one-year inflation outlook climbed to 4.6% from 4.0% in August — its steepest reading since June, even as it beat the preliminary 47.8 print.
stories.explain: The Fed treats this survey's inflation-expectations component as an early-warning gauge for whether the public is starting to 'de-anchor' — building rising prices into their own wage demands and spending decisions, which can turn a temporary price shock into a self-reinforcing spiral. A jump like today's 60-bp rise, layered on top of an already-hawkish Fed, is precisely the kind of data point that hardens the case for the October hike the futures market is now pricing at 71%.

stories.headline: NO. 1 TEXAS SURVIVES AT TENNESSEE 20-17 BEHIND FIVE-SACK PERFORMANCE
stories.body: Top-ranked Texas held off No. 14 Tennessee 20-17 at Neyland Stadium as edge rusher Colin Simmons tied the program record with five sacks. The result headlined a stacked Week 4 Saturday slate that also included No. 4 Ole Miss at No. 21 Florida and Colorado at Baylor.

stories.headline: STEPHEN CURRY AGREES TO 2-YEAR, $116M EXTENSION TO STAY WITH WARRIORS
stories.body: Curry and Golden State agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension running through 2028-29 — below the roughly $136 million he could have commanded — pushing the total value of his current deal to about $178.6 million. The move came as Dallas held its media day previewing a Kyrie Irving-Cooper Flagg pairing under new coach and GM structure, with camps opening league-wide September 29.

stories.headline: COWBOYS HEAD TO BRAZIL FOR NFL'S FIRST-EVER RIO GAME AS QB INJURY WAVE CONTINUES
stories.body: Dallas travels to Rio de Janeiro to face Lamar Jackson and the Ravens in the league's first regular-season game in Brazil, while Week 3 is reshaped by quarterback injuries — the Bears could be without both Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent, and the Giants' Jaxson Dart was placed on injured reserve with a knee injury, handing the start back to Jameis Winston.

stories.headline: FLORIDA TOPS UPDATED PRESEASON TOP 25 AS TEAMS OPEN CAMP
stories.body: CBS Sports' updated 2026-27 preseason Top 25 And 1 has defending-nucleus Florida at No. 1, followed by Duke, Michigan, Illinois and UConn, with Arkansas, Gonzaga, Texas and Arizona rounding out the top nine. Rankings have shifted throughout the offseason as transfer portal moves and NBA draft decisions settled roster.

deepDive.title: How a 71% Fed Hike Probability Actually Gets Calculated
content: Today's watchlist item — "CME FedWatch odds of a hike near 71-73%" — is one of the most-quoted numbers in financial media, yet it isn't a poll or a survey of economists. It's a probability backed out of real money changing hands in the fed funds futures market, and understanding how that back-out works explains why the number moves almost every trading day even between FOMC meetings, and why it moved from 8.8% to over 70% in barely a month once the data started turning.

The mechanism starts with 30-day fed funds futures contracts, whose settlement price is tied to the average effective fed funds rate over a given month. If the market is certain the Fed holds rates steady, that futures price implies exactly the current rate. Any deviation from that no-change price reveals how much of a rate move traders are pricing in, and CME's FedWatch tool inverts that math: it takes the futures price, compares it to the two possible post-meeting rates (hold or +25 bps), and solves for the implied probability weighting between them, then chains that across contracts to build the full curve of expected moves out through several meetings.

What most people miss is that this is a market-implied probability, not a forecast in the everyday sense — it reflects the marginal price at which futures traders are willing to transact, which can be distorted by hedging flows, liquidity, and positioning, not just pure rate-view. That's why the 1994 tightening cycle still gets taught as a cautionary tale: Alan Greenspan's Fed delivered a 75-bp hike that futures markets had been pricing far below fair odds of just weeks earlier, and the mispricing broke bond desks and even helped sink Orange County, California into bankruptcy. Implied odds are a real-time read of positioning, not a guarantee.

For Chris's watchlist, that distinction matters heading into October 27-28: a 71-73% implied probability means roughly three more percentage points of upside surprise probability is still sitting on the table if incoming data — like next week's PCE or early-October payrolls — comes in hotter than expected, and every point that number moves will show up first in the 2-year yield, which is the part of the curve most directly tied to near-term Fed policy. Watch whether it breaks decisively above 80% or slips back toward 60% as new data lands over the next month.
